[iris/grug] Save a final checkpoint before preemption kills training
topics.body:
Iris's multi-GPU launcher forwards SIGTERM to every training rank, then escalates to SIGKILL after 10 seconds. Grug's training loop has no checkpoint-on-SIGTERM path; it forces a final checkpoint only after normal completion. A gracefully preempted job therefore resumes from the last periodic checkpoint and loses intervening updates.

Saving on preemption needs time to finish a training step, coordinate every rank at the same completed step, and durably commit the checkpoint. The launcher deadline and Kubernetes pod termination grace must both cover that operation.

Done when:

- When all ranks receive SIGTERM with sufficient grace, they finish the same training step, save its model/optimizer/data-position state, and wait for durable commit before exiting.
- Pod and launcher shutdown deadlines support a configurable grace period. Start validation at 60 seconds and measure whether that provides sufficient margin; this is a proposed starting point, not a validated guarantee.
- Controlled preemption during a step and during an existing asynchronous save produces a complete checkpoint of the final completed step. Retried training preserves the run ID and checkpoint root, restores the recorded step and data position, and ignores incomplete writes.
- Shutdown remains bounded when a rank fails or storage stalls. Ordinary application failures retain their original error handling.

Code: [launcher timeout](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/1d6cca120eeebfe2446bf690e8e8dbb6d4559422/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/multigpu_main.py#L61-L66), [signal forwarding and forced termination](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/1d6cca120eeebfe2446bf690e8e8dbb6d4559422/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/multigpu_main.py#L195-L217), [Grug final checkpoint handling](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/1d6cca120eeebfe2446bf690e8e8dbb6d4559422/experiments/grug/fast_track/train.py#L978-L1003).

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Current Grug loops force and await a final checkpoint only after normal completion; SIGTERM reaches the ranks through Iris's supervisor and can terminate a rank before that path runs. The supervisor escalates after 10 seconds, the worker kill path defaults to 5 seconds, and the task Pod manifest sets no termination grace. Levanter writes checkpoint metadata after the async serialization callback, but `wait_until_finished()` also waits for background deletion, which can consume the shutdown budget after the checkpoint is committed. No open PR matched #10761 or SIGTERM checkpointing.

**Relevant code**
- [`multigpu_main.py#L61-L64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/hooks/multigpu_main.py#L61-L64) — 10-second kill deadline.
- [`train.py#L683-L705`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/train.py#L683-L705) — periodic and normal-exit saves.
- [`checkpoint.py#L676-L680`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py#L676-L680) — commit wait includes deletion.
- [`task_attempt.py#L405-L426`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/task_attempt.py#L405-L426) — worker force-kill deadline.
- [`tasks.py#L965-L974`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L965-L974) — task Pod spec.

# Proposed Fix

1. Add an explicit per-job preemption grace to the Fray/Iris request path. Use it for the multi-GPU supervisor and worker stop deadline, and stamp `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` on task Pods with margin beyond the supervisor deadline. Keep a finite hard stop. Start validation at 60 seconds; choose the production value from measured step, pending-save, commit, and teardown times.
2. In the Grug training loops, install a SIGTERM handler that only records shutdown intent. At each completed-step boundary, have every rank participate in the same stop decision and verify the same step before beginning another batch. On preemption, skip optional callbacks, finish any in-flight async save, and commit a permanent checkpoint of the final completed model, optimizer, and step state. If that step already committed, reuse it. Keep ordinary training exceptions on their current failure path.
3. Give checkpoint callers a commit-only wait so background checkpoint pruning cannot hold up graceful exit. Retain metadata as the completion marker; verify restore ignores an interrupted write and resumes from the recorded step and data position. Keep the launcher's run ID and checkpoint root stable across retries.
4. Add local process tests for SIGTERM during a step, SIGTERM during an async save, a failed rank, and a stalled save. Then run a controlled multi-rank GPU preemption and retry, measure shutdown latency against the configured budget, and confirm restored step/data position and checkpoint contents. A rank or storage failure must end through the finite kill deadline.

Open question for implementation: which Grug entrypoints should opt in initially? The base and hero loops both have this completion-only save pattern; the hero run is the clearest first validation target.
@weaverbot just hit all the grug entry points. It should be generic enough to be a few lines of code per variant.

🤖 Opened [PR #10774](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10774) for the Grug entry points. Training ranks agree on the final completed step after SIGTERM, finish any pending asynchronous save, and commit that step's model, optimizer, and data-position state before exit. The change also carries a configurable grace period through the GPU launcher, Iris worker, and Kubernetes Pod; Grug starts at 60 seconds plus five seconds for teardown.

Focused Grug, checkpoint, and Iris tests pass, including all 19 worker reconciliation tests after updating their container fakes for graceful SIGTERM. A local CPU restart probe restored step 6 and data position 192. The affected test run reached 5,124 passes, 10 skips, and 5 expected failures before its 600-second pytest session timeout; it also had one visualization-test worker crash. The mandatory lint and advisory review pass with no findings.

The proposed 60-second value is **not yet validated** against a multi-GPU step or remote checkpoint commit. A controlled two-rank H100 preemption job was rejected before creation because the submitter lacks the required CoreWeave object-storage credentials. PR #10774 is therefore part of this issue; the GPU preemption and restart check remains before closing it.

🤖 [PR #10774](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10774) now covers the Grug training entry points. Ranks stop at the same completed step after SIGTERM and wait for a permanent model, optimizer, and data-position checkpoint, including when an asynchronous save is pending. A preempted trainer exits with SIGTERM status after the commit so Iris can retry it. The launcher, worker, and Pod use a configurable 1–110 second grace; Grug starts at 60 seconds with five extra seconds for teardown. CI is green.

A [controlled two-H100 Grug base probe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10774#issuecomment-6501275454) preempted during a step and during an asynchronous save. Both ranks committed completed step 3 and exited with status 143. Restarting with the same run ID and checkpoint root restored the saved model, optimizer, and example position 12; the run reached step 6 with bitwise-identical state to an uninterrupted baseline and ignored a newer incomplete checkpoint. Supervisor exit took 8.75 and 10.22 seconds. A stalled commit was force-killed after 61.12 seconds; an injected rank failure ended the group within 0.86 seconds.

The probe checkpoint was about 0.94 MiB. Production-size checkpoint timing, automatic Iris task retry, live worker/Pod grace, and the other variants on GPU remain unvalidated. The proposed 60-second production margin needs a representative-size measurement, so this PR remains **part of #10761** rather than closing the issue.

After 12 hours of PR monitoring, the PR remains open with green CI and review required. An approval was dismissed without a stated reason. Review/merge and the representative-size measurement are the remaining actions.

[grug] Clip the hero gradient norm at 1.0 and prepare its handoff
topics.head: c1c8adaa795c6b87a378c551152c7bbb065e4afb
topics.body:
Clip the hero's total gradient norm to 1.0 in the train step, and prepare the handoff to the clipped run `hero-gradclip-step<N>k`. The running `hero-ctx16k-step257k` is unaffected until it is relaunched from this commit. Merge only after N is filled in at cutover.

#10677 traced the hero's gradient spikes to single 16K sequences. They are long, repetitive, sink-less windows. At the exact bf16 forward state, their per-sequence gradient is enormous, and it compounds from the upper layers down to the embeddings. Since step 340000 the median `grad/norm/total` is 0.501.

Step 352190 reached 4.49. Step 353060 reached 20.84 (41.6x the median):
- Layers 0–26 were 50–208x their recent medians, with the peak at layer 22. Layers 29–47 were 1.3–2.3x.
- `token_embed` was 138x.
- The loss jumped from 1.018 at step 353060 to 1.101 at step 353061, the only rise above 0.05 since step 351000.
- It recovered over about 50 steps. The mean loss was 1.018 over 353040–353059, 1.073 over 353061–353065, 1.030 over 353076–353085, and 1.018 over 353101–353140.

The norm is logged only every 10th step, so spikes on the other nine steps are never seen.

The train step now computes `optax.global_norm` over the whole gradient, the quantity W&B logs as `grad/norm/total`. Above `max_grad_norm`, it scales every leaf by `max_norm / norm` before the optimizer. At or below the limit, every leaf is multiplied by exactly 1.
- Every step logs `train/grad_norm` (pre-clip) and `train/grad_clipped`. The watch's `grad/norm/*` keep their pre-clip meaning and their 10-step cadence.
- `HERO_MAX_GRAD_NORM = 1.0` is required by `hero_grug_trainer_config` and set for the d6144 rung. The narrow ladder rungs stay unclipped.
- `launch_diagnostics --max-grad-norm` defaults to 1.0.

The clip is outside the optimizer, so the opt_state pytree and checkpoint layout do not change, and current hero checkpoints restore as they are. The optimizer's existing per-group `max_grad_norm` would not: it prepends `clip_by_global_norm` to each muonh/adamh/adam chain. That moves every opt_state key, for example from `inner_states['adam'].inner_state[0].mu` to `.inner_state[1].mu` (checked with `jax.eval_shape`). It also clips each group on its own norm rather than the total. That path is left unused.

`current_run.py` and `trigger_hero.sh` follow the #9960 and #10101 handoffs, with N left as `REPLACE_BEFORE_DEPLOYMENT`. The script refuses to fork or launch with that value. The three values are:
- `hero-gradclip-step<N/1000>k`;
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-ctx16k-step257k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-N`;
- `hero-ctx16k-step257k?_step=<N-1>`.

The cutover follows the README's "Hero cutovers and W&B lineage" and `code-cutover.md`:
1. Request a permanent checkpoint from the old run's training-control endpoint, with header `X-Levanter-Training-Control: request-permanent-checkpoint`. The hero's code at `eadf76a1bc` wires `TrainingDashboard` to `Checkpointer.request_checkpoint`. That maps the request to PERMANENT retention, and the next step saves `step-N` to the permanent root with `is_temporary: false`.
2. Wait for that `metadata.json` with `"is_temporary": false`, and confirm on the parent that `_step` N−1 is `global_step` N−1. It was at 353999.
3. Fill in N and merge.
4. Let the old run record the 200-step matched control window after `step-N` before stopping it.
5. Run `trigger_hero.sh fork-wandb`, stop the old coordinator, then run `trigger_hero.sh launch`.
6. Apply the agreed gates. Rollback relaunches `hero-ctx16k-step257k` at `eadf76a1bc`.

Two one-rack resume tests restored the hero's permanent `step-354000` read-only on cw-us-east-08a at production priority. Settings:
- global batch 256 (2816 / 11);
- the hero's optimizer sized for batch 2816 (beta2 0.95, epsilon 6.04e-15), with MuonH and Adam learning rates × sqrt(1/11) (0.000992 and 0.000229);
- clip 1.0;
- output under `s3://marin-us-east-08a/tmp/ttl=30d/hero-clip-resume-test/`.

rt1 ran `f00d75cff3`, and rt2 ran `0d56a910a5`. Both set the batch-2816 sizing and the LR scale with temporary diagnostic flags (`--optimizer-batch-size 2816 --lr-scale 0.3015`). The flags are not part of this PR; branch state `2f7e57ae26` has them. The clip and the train step are unchanged since those runs.

| | [hero-clip-rt1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-clip-rt1) | [hero-clip-rt2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-clip-rt2) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| steps | 354000–354032, cancelled | 354000–354019 |
| loss at 354000 | 1.014783 (hero 1.022036 on its full batch) | 1.014783 |
| mean loss 354001–354019 | 1.023 (hero 1.017) | 1.023, within 1.2e-4 of rt1 per step |
| median `train/grad_norm` | 0.39, logged every step | 0.39, logged every step |
| clip fired | 354012 (1.041), 354029 (1.975) | 354002 (3.228) |
| step time, MFU | 13.4 s, 31.5% (hero 13.7–18.0 s) | 13.2 s, 31.8% |
| peak memory | 123.21 GiB | 123.21 GiB |

Results:
- No step produced a NaN.
- `train/grad_clipped` equals `train/grad_norm > 1` on every row.
- `train/grad_norm` equals the watch's `grad/norm/total` on every 10th step.
- rt1's first attempt lost two ranks to a tokenizer-staging race in `/tmp/levanter_tokenizers` after a clean 188 s restore; its automatic retry trained.

The two runs see identical batches from identical weights, yet their spikes land on different steps. This matches #10677's finding that a spike sits at an ill-conditioned point that rounding moves. The fire rate at batch 256 does not predict the hero's: one pathological sequence carries 11x more weight in a 256-row mean. At the hero's median of 0.50, the clip should fire on spikes like 352190 and 353060.

New CPU tests cover:
- the clip's bitwise no-op and its global rescale;
- the clipped train step;
- restoring an unclipped checkpoint into a clipping run.

The `tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py`, `test_scaling_ladder.py`, and `test_grug_variant_contracts.py` suites pass (110 tests), and `./infra/pre-commit.py --all-files` is clean. `--review` flagged three issues:
- a positional tuple return, now the `ClippedGradients` NamedTuple;
- rollout context in the clip constant's comment, now removed;
- a bare `"d6144"` literal, left as is because the file already compares against it in several places.

Part of #10677.

comments.body:
🤖 Holistic review of 2f7e57ae26f741ba7f41be1a4f88a9fa5a0ef229.

This change adds a global gradient-norm clip at 1.0 to the hero train step. It also lets the next hero start from the old run's hourly temporary checkpoint instead of waiting for a permanent one. Both pieces are correct as written, and the eight new CPU tests pass locally. The temporary-checkpoint procedure conflicts with an open PR that changes how a stopped hero exits, so the second of the two to merge needs a docs update.

**Clip.** Before this change, the hero had no gradient clip. The optimizer's per-group `max_grad_norm` would prepend `clip_by_global_norm` to each chain and change the opt_state layout. `clip_by_total_norm` (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py:959`) runs in `_make_train_step` instead. It scales every leaf by `max_norm / norm` when the norm exceeds the limit and multiplies by exactly 1 otherwise, so checkpoint layout is unchanged. The watch still receives `raw_grads`, so `grad/norm/*` keep their pre-clip meaning. `train/grad_norm` and `train/grad_clipped` are logged on every step. `hero_grug_trainer_config` now requires `max_grad_norm`. The ladder passes `HERO_MAX_GRAD_NORM` only for `d6144`, and diagnostics default to it. Infinite norms scale to zero, and NaN passes through unchanged, just as before.

**Temporary handoff.** Before, a handoff had to use a permanent checkpoint, because temporary checkpoints expire after three days. Now `permanent_checkpoint_on_resume` runs `on_step(force=True)` right after the restore. It writes `step-N` with `is_temporary: false` into the child's own `base_path`, but only when `discover_checkpoint_candidates(base_path)` finds nothing there. A retry therefore finds the copy and skips the write. A retry after the source expires also restores from the child's own root, because `restore_grug_state_from_checkpoint` treats a missing search root as having no candidates. The forced save's commit callback only prunes the child's own recorded temporaries, so nothing in the parent's tree is touched. `checkpoints._PARENT_CHECKPOINT_PATTERN` already matches the `tmp/ttl=3d/.../<run>/<version>/checkpoints/step-N` layout, so lineage listing works with a temporary source.

**Evidence and limits.** I ran the new tests locally (`-k "clip or resume or fresh_run or lineage"`): 8 passed. The one-rack restore runs rt1 and rt2 on `step-354000` are claims in the body; I did not reproduce them. The body says merging waits for the `REPLACE_BEFORE_DEPLOYMENT` values in `current_run.py` and `trigger_hero.sh`. Until those are filled in, `CURRENT_HERO_RUN_ID` on main names a run that does not exist.

**Findings**

- **1. Related PR:** `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/README.md:143` #10774 ("Save completed steps on preemption") changes `moe_hero_ep/train.py` so a SIGTERM'd trainer calls `checkpointer.save_final_checkpoint`. That call is a forced permanent save at the stop step. Its commit callback runs `_prune_temporary_checkpoints(0)`, which deletes the run's recorded temporary checkpoints. Suppose a hero runs with #10774's code and is stopped as in step 2 of the new "hand off from a temporary checkpoint" procedure. It writes a permanent `step-M` (M ≥ N) and deletes the temporary `step-N` the procedure tells the operator to hand off from. This PR is time-sensitive and should land first; the current parent runs `eadf76a1bc` and is unaffected. When #10774 lands, it should update this README section and `.agents/skills/manage-hero-run/references/code-cutover.md`: for a run that includes graceful preemption, the handoff is the permanent checkpoint written at the stop step. The temporary-checkpoint path then applies only to runs without that code.

The PR is now the clip plus the run-id placeholders, with HANDOFF_CHECKPOINT pointing at a permanent step-N requested through the training-control endpoint. The resume tests ran at f00d75cff3 / 0d56a910a5 (the options exist at 2f7e57ae26); the clip and train step are unchanged since. Lint, --review and the affected CPU tests (110) pass at ce36eb112f.

topics.head: 04fcd7c0c3ad80fbe8dc822375bb8d9ea1698b12
topics.body:
Use the Snowball inventory serving profile that reproduced identical results on the fixed 100-task panel: greedy evaluation with seed 20261020, batch-invariant arithmetic, prefix caching disabled, and one scheduled sequence per inference worker. DP8/EP8/TP1/PP1, chunked prefill with an 8192-token budget, CUDA graphs, the 24576-token context, and the 8192-token reply limit stay in place. The sequence cap also applies to training generation and reduces concurrency; throughput has not been measured.

Preserve explicit evaluation sampling fields at the HTTP boundary and forward the chunked-prefill setting to vLLM. Training requests for behavior logprobs still reject a sampling distribution that differs from the configured training sampling distribution.

Six evaluations across four fresh engine startups produced identical prompt and response tokens, text, grades, and recorded outcomes: four direct-SFT evaluations and two normal Megatron initial evaluations with NCCL expert_block weight transfer and zero optimizer steps. Each generated 469450 response tokens with mean rollout reward 0.2002 on H100s with Grug-67B and vLLM revision 39e62869693c. Outputs still varied under concurrent batching with batch invariance initialized, prefix caching disabled, and eager execution enabled. These results cover the fixed 100-task panel; they do not establish universal bitwise determinism or an exclusive GPU-operator cause. All GPU evaluations and diagnostics used a separate diagnostic branch; this exact PR head has not been run on GPUs.

topics.body:
Hero run started on August 19th. This should be a terse log of status events and interventions since then.

```
./experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/trigger_hero.sh
```

comments.body:
August 20th: noticed that we are OOMing every ~3 hours.

We attempted interventions to adjust XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.83 (giving XLA more memory). This made things worse. 

--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor seems to be another promising tunable. Adjusting to 0.88 from the default 0.95 didn't help. Testing with 0.85 now.

In theory fraction 0.83 with slop 88 strictly dominates the baseline, as a followup to test if the lowered thresholds don't hold.

04:06:44 UTC — at step ~2359 (loss 1.78), GPUs on node s9vrxs64 (task 9, with tasks 4/8 in the same rack failing alongside) hit `CUDA_ERROR_NVLINK_UNCORRECTABLE: uncorrectable NVLink error detected during the execution`
For completeness of the log: on August 19th 8:30pm PT, step 164, manual test of resume failed due to host OOM, fixed and resumed via https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480

We observed periodic host OOMs after several checkpoints. https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/200 . Restarting with the following changes:

1. Tensorstore restore parallelism bounded by a fixed budget
2. Checkpoint offload cache to 16GB
3. malloc_trim() calls after each checkpoint

in theory 2 will make checkpoints faster (fully async), and 3 will prevent the host OOM recurrence

`malloc_trim` was still inconsistently resulting in OOMs during checkpointing. Restarting on main with the jemalloc changes in.

Restores were hitting single worker stalls. Merged and running with #8584 . First restore after this change was successful, though it might have been luck/caching.

🤖 Relaunched after a checkpoint-time OOM

The `coord-fast-restore` instance OOMed while saving step 11252 at 22:57 UTC. Iris retried the 176-task child, so the root was cancelled to avoid overlapping production gangs.

Replacement: https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fpower%2Fhero-12d8b6f0-dee637-coord-memfix

The replacement uses `main` at `8aaeb40fe2dd152734801edafe474f8e52ef78f8`, the existing `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` run ID, size `d6144`, version `2026.08.19.2`, and the existing W&B/output lineage. The launcher will select the newest complete checkpoint. The coordinator uses JAX port `32615`.

Current status: the coordinator is running and waiting for the Marin step lock held by the previous instance to expire. Next check is lock acquisition, 176-task gang dispatch, and checkpoint restore.

🤖 Memory sampling on the current `coord-memfix` instance isolates checkpoint-correlated retained RSS to writer tasks 0–127. Their median floor rose 11.7 GiB after the first save and 4.4 GiB after the second; tasks 128–175 stayed on the baseline slope. Each writer rank was assigned about 9.5–10.2 GiB, and `/proc` attributes the retained difference to anonymous memory across the four child Python processes.

The run contains #8609. The signature matches its documented persistent CUDA pinned-host BFC pool cost. The smaller second increment does not support projecting a fixed 30 GiB leak per save.

Incident record: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/227

🤖 Correction after tracing the current checkpoint path: the long-lived `GlobalAsyncCheckpointManager` keeps the completed TensorStore commit futures in `_commit_futures`; `wait_until_finished()` joins but does not clear them, and the writes allow indefinite source-buffer references. This mechanism predates #8609 and plausibly retains one staged checkpoint share per writer rank. PR #8599 contained a reviewed post-join cleanup for these futures, but that part did not land with #8609. The pinned-host BFC pool in #8609 remains an additional allocator-level floor that clearing the manager cannot purge. Updated evidence and safe cleanup boundaries: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/227

🤖 At 08:52:52 UTC, training task 8 OOMed during checkpoint serialization. The 2 GB coordinator OOMed 16 seconds later. Its zero failure retry budget then stopped the 176-task child job.

Evidence: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/232

PR #8617 adds the production trigger with a 4 GB coordinator and a failure retry budget of 1000: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8617

Resumed job: https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frav%2Fhero-12d8b6f0-dee637-coord-84a0012f%2Fgrug-train-hero-12d8b6f0-dee637

🤖 The loader-cache ablation is complete. On two trays with the Harrier mixture, global batch 1024, and sequence length 4096, the profiler-free 1 GB/process arm delivered 0.937 batches/s including cold start versus 0.956 batches/s at 125 GB/process. The hero runs at 19.9 s/step (0.050 batches/s), so the 1 GB cap has 18.6x headroom and bounds the decoded cache near 0.923 GiB/process. Report: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/235

🤖 Attempt 0 failed after node `s6htxs64` lost connectivity. At 16:53:31 UTC, JAX reported that process IDs 333–335 had stopped sending heartbeats; startup logs map those IDs to local ranks 1–3 of Iris task 83 on that node. Kubernetes marked the node `NotReady` 11 seconds later, CoreWeave cordoned it for `ConnectivityUpdateTime`, and the node rebooted at 17:07. No OOM, CUDA, NCCL, or training exception preceded the failure. The tenant-visible events do not identify why connectivity was lost.

Iris atomically retried the 176-task gang. Attempt 1 resumed at step 27,000 and was training when checked at 17:15 UTC.

Incident record: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/270

🤖 Echo incident record: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/310

Attempt 1 stalled after step 50195 when task 83 host s55sxs64 / 10.186.210.49 logged a local IB port error and later entered IBFlappingSingleNodeInterface. Attempt 2 restored step 50191 and reached step 50207 with clean telemetry and RAS. No live run action is required.

🤖 Hero backend swap to ragged all-to-all (main `8e48cdb3ca`), 2026-09-02. The pooled-wave hero `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` was stopped at step 54262 (22:27Z). The replacement runs under a new run id, `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k`, resuming full state from the old run's `step-54000` permanent checkpoint via `--initialize-from-checkpoint` (#8868) so the old run's W&B history and checkpoint tree stay intact. Launched 23:26Z; first step 00:03Z after a 15-min cold data-loader fetch and a ~14-min cold compile. Through step 54054 on the same batches as the control: loss tracks the old run step for step at a constant −0.006 nats (dropless), drop fraction 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.3%, 16.8 s/step vs 18.5. Go/no-go at step 54200 (~01:00Z) from the side-by-side report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA== Rollback, if needed, is `trigger_hero.sh` at `04751985c7`, which resumes the old run from step-54000. Capacity-limited eval is off on the new run (#8859, #8861); dashboards move to the dropless eval in #8862.

🤖 Rolled back at 01:15Z. The ragged hero (`hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k`) hung twice: step 54071 on attempt 0 (after 70 clean steps at 23.4% MFU, loss matching the old run step for step) and step 54001 on attempt 1, each time on one rack's EP domain, with no error logged; the progress watchdog killed each attempt after 15 min. Evidence and analysis in #8870. The old code (`04751985c7`, run `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637`) was relaunched from the same `step-54000` permanent checkpoint at 01:15Z as `/marin/hero-12d8b6f0-dee637-coord-e3052688`; its checkpoint tree and W&B history were never written by the ragged run. Net cost of the trial: ~3 h of the 11 racks and the old run's steps 54001–54262.

🤖 Rollback verified. `/marin/hero-12d8b6f0-dee637-coord-e3052688` (`04751985c7`) restored `step-54000` at 01:20Z and is training at ~17 s/step with loss matching its own earlier trajectory step for step (54002: 1.24686 vs 1.2465; 54008: 1.2574 vs 1.2574). Steps 54001–54262 are a replay of what the pooled-wave run had already trained before the swap, so the W&B run shows no new rows until it passes 54262 (~02:40Z); finelog/Grafana carry every step now. No config change from before the swap; the next permanent checkpoint is step 60000.

🤖 Paused for the #8870 debugging window and redeployed from main. A checkpoint was forced through the training-control endpoint before the cancel, so the pause cost about one step instead of the ~131 (~44 min, ~515 GPU-hours) that killing at a random point in the hourly temporary-checkpoint cycle would have discarded: `step-58014` committed 23:13:13Z and was verified complete (`manifest.json`, `manifest.ocdbt`, `metadata.json`, 28,098 objects, 5.36 TB). `/marin/hero-12d8b6f0-dee637-coord-e3052688` was cancelled at 23:14:12Z having last logged step 58.0k at loss 1.22.

The window ran 11 racks from 23:16Z to 00:40Z across two jobs and did not reproduce the hang: 164 steps then 71, 235 in total, at the hero's exact shape restored from the same `step-54000` the two failed attempts used. Details in #8870.

Redeployed at 00:41:36Z from a pristine worktree at `origin/main` `023ed7a24d` as `/marin/hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k-coord-95c15d9b`, run id `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k`, submitted with `IRIS_USER=marin`. It carries two changes relative to the paused run: the pooled-wave fallback (#8884, which the paused run was already effectively running) and gate/router weight decay on by default at 0.02 annealed linearly to zero (#8833). The launch args were diffed against the paused run's own recorded argv and match on every field except run id, job name, `--initialize-from-checkpoint`, and the `--system-reason` string.

Resume verified: the gang placed in ~80 s, 177 tasks, and the restore names `step-58014` under the temporary root rather than falling back to the `step-54000` permanent, which would have discarded ~4,000 steps. First step 00:50:12Z; now training at ~18.4 s/step, MFU ~21%, loss ~1.24, continuous with the 1.22-1.25 before the pause, and logging to W&B as `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k`.

Net cost: ~96 min of the 11 racks, of which ~84 was the window and ~9 startup.

Note for #8833: that experiment's launcher originally handed off from `step-54000`; #8890 repointed it at `step-58014` so the relaunch would not discard the day of training since. Its control is therefore the paused hero's own trajectory from 58014, not the step-54000 one.

🤖 Plan for today's redeployment of the hero on the ragged all-to-all transport, 2026-09-09. The live run `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k` (commit `0908920c86`) is at step ~81.5k at 19.8 s/step, loss ~1.23.

Sequence: merge #8959 (QuACK 0.6.4, the grouped-GEMM scheduler fix) and #9043 (ragged transport and fp32 weights on device back as the hero default, reverting #8884), then force a checkpoint on the live run through the training-control endpoint about 70 minutes before the cutover, mark its metadata non-temporary so the hourly temporary save does not prune it, open the launcher PR pointing `trigger_hero.sh` at it under run id `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step<N>k`, let the old run train 200 steps past it as the paired control, cancel the old coordinator, and launch main from a pristine worktree as `IRIS_USER=marin`. Waiting for the next permanent checkpoint was rejected: step-84000 lands at ~07:00Z tomorrow and step-90000 on Thursday, and a forced checkpoint costs one step (the step-58014 precedent).

The new run carries, relative to the live one: the ragged transport with fp32 weights on device (#9043), one train-step executable per rank (#8911), the balanced ragged device kernel wheel (#8976), QuACK 0.6.4 (#8959), and the cross-entropy tile and FA4 padding fixes (#8960, #8961). The root cause of #8870 is still open; the strongest lead is a fabric fault on the racks that land at replica indices 8-10, which the trial cannot avoid.

Gate over the 200-step window against the old run on the same batches: loss within bf16 noise of the control after the ~0.006 nat dropless offset, drop fraction below 1e-3, MFU at or above the control's ~21%, no hang, retry, or watchdog. Anything short of that rolls back at once by relaunching `trigger_hero.sh` at `0908920c86`, which resumes the old run's own newest checkpoint. Runbook scripts (preflight with an NVLink counter sweep, cancel, launch, monitor, rollback) are being dry-run read-only against the cluster. A W&B report with both run sets over the trial window will be linked here before launch, along with each transition: forced checkpoint, cancel, launch, first steps, go/no-go.

topics.body:
Honor `PRESERVE_CHILDREN` when a parent's own tasks succeed, so asynchronous exports and evaluations can finish after their coordinator exits. Successful parents previously killed every unfinished descendant regardless of the policy.

This extends the preemption policy introduced in #3685 to normal completion. Multi-task jobs default to `PRESERVE_CHILDREN`, so their unfinished children now continue after success; callers that rely on cleanup must explicitly use `TERMINATE_CHILDREN` or cancel the job tree. Single-task defaults and explicit cancellation still terminate descendants. Document these lifetimes and the separate coordinator, child-execution and application deadlines during Kueue queueing.

Controller journeys reproduce the failure for one-task and four-task parents and verify surviving descendants can complete. The focused hierarchy and transition suites pass all 134 tests; the affected suite passes 2,072 tests.

Part of #10768.

topics.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. I think most likely scenario is the hero runs around 2 percent dropping, but up to 8 percent seems plausible bsaed on the data at 4k seqlen.

Also noting- the d2048 scaling ladder rung failed at 81%. Chose not to resume to add more time to Hero Run. The dynamics look clear from the first 81 percent, and we can cleanly extrapolate the last 19%. From a practical perspective, we will not actually be running the end of the run at 4k seqlen, and the datamix may update midrun. So the utility of the scaling law is more around the first 50 percent of the run and ensuring the projection is reasonably within expectation (which it is).

From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

| FP32 operands | `0.00000416` | `0.00002373` | all 324 matched | 18.20 ms | 23.26 ms |

The isolated timing covers only the saved-input router dot and gradient. It is not a whole-step measurement.

🤖 One-rack measurement ahead of the planned 4K to 8K switch, restoring the step-180000 checkpoint at the hero's per-rack load of 4.19M tokens per step, with 3 seeds × 100 steps per arm: 8K trains at 1.6% fewer tokens/s than 4K, and the fraction of expert assignments dropped rises 4.5×, from 1.9e-4 to 8.3e-4, all on the sender side. 16K costs 3.1% of tokens/s and 16× the drops. Setup, W&B runs, and caveats are in #9615. The main caveats: one-rack drop fractions at 4K are about 2× the 11-rack hero's, and each run covers only 100 steps after the switch.

I posted an independent, pre-registered forecast of the final dropless Paloma macro, with intervals, in #9977: median 2.035, 80% [2.023, 2.047], using data through step 227,999. That puts the run on track to match or slightly beat the Aug 19 pre-registration. It also traces most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap to whether lm_head FLOPs are counted in compute. cc @ClassicLarry @dlwh

**An independent forecast of the final loss, with a law found from the data (no fixed form)**

I forecast the run's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`: the last eval logged in the lineage at step 387,000 or later, as W&B records it (expected at 16K packing). I used only public W&B data, up to step 302,999 (snapshot of 2026-10-21, 22:58 UTC).

| forecast | data | value | 90 % interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | ladder + the hero's own evals | **1.979** | [1.965, 1.994] |
| B | ladder only | **1.935** | [1.915, 1.963] |

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.
- B is the ladder-only law at the hero's compute and the end of training.
- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

B is 0.10 below the Aug 19 pre-registration from the same ladder, because the law NAI found has no fixed floor.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

A measurement for anyone checking forecasts made while the evals packed at 4K (Marin's Aug 19 forecast of 2.039, and mine in #9977): the switch to 16K lowered the Paloma macro by about 0.031 on nearly the same weights. The `qk16k-a1-step252k` arm restored step 252,000 with the hero's post-switch settings (16K, `qk_mult` 1.48) and logged 2.0929 and 2.0926 at steps 252,049 and 252,099, against 2.1234 for the hero's 4K eval of that checkpoint, logged at step 251,999. With `qk_mult` left at 1.3 (`qk16k-a0-step252k`), the drop is about 0.028. The hero's own step from 254,999 to 257,999 looks smaller (0.024) because WikiText's dip at 254,999 lowered the last 4K eval; without WikiText it is 0.032 over those 3,000 steps. So a 4K-era forecast scored against the 16K final value, as in H1 and H4 of the forecast linked above, starts about 0.03 high from the packing change alone. The offset may also drift over the remaining 16K training, so if it's cheap, one 4K eval of the final checkpoint would let these forecasts be checked at the 4K packing they were built on. How I'll compare the forecasts at the end, fixed before phase 2, is in [this addendum](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/phase2-plan-2026-10-22/addenda/2026-10-22_phase2_plan.md).

We will re-eval all checkpoints at 4k seqlen once the run is done, for those who have been tracking separate predictions. (Though a model trained at 4k->16k->65k may eval slightly differently at 4k than one that stayed at 4k the whole run, so not making any claims from our end on where that will end up).

A heads-up for the hero's planned 262K extension (#10618): with evals packed at the training context, Paloma's PTB and WikiText-103 val sets are each shorter than one 262,144-token sequence, so they yield no eval data ([`tokens // seq_len`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L93)). Their losses are then logged as 0.0 and the Paloma group macro skips them ([eval.py#L634-L636](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L634-L636)), so `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` silently becomes a 14-subset mean: at current values a jump of about +0.06 (about 3%), enough to trip `eval_regressed`. The top-level `macro_loss` instead averages the zeros in ([eval.py#L611](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L611)), about −0.14 on the hero's 23 tags. The 67B's 65K→262K switch, with the same tokenizer and Paloma files, shows both: from step 155,999 ([65K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step141k)) to 156,000 ([262K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k)), `eval/paloma/macro_loss` rose 2.1774 → 2.2150 while the other 14 subsets moved +0.0004, and `eval/macro_loss` fell 2.0260 → 1.8607 (2.0379 without the zeros). Either fix is small: mask zero-token tags in the top-level macro as the group macros already do, or keep all 16 subsets by setting `GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len` (#9890) to 65,536 for the 262K phase.

🤖 Confirmed in the current source: [`TokenSeqDataset.async_len`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L92-L93) drops partial sequences, and [`TaggedEvaluator.evaluate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L608-L636) includes empty tags in the overall macro while excluding them from group macros. I will exclude zero-token tags from the overall loss and bits-per-byte macros, and cap eval packing at 65,536 tokens in the Hero scaling-ladder and diagnostic launchers so the 262K phase retains all 16 Paloma subsets. This is a separate follow-up to #10618; it requires no live run change.

topics.title: [grug] Hero attention: FP32 saved O vs baseline, 1-rack 50-step head-to-head
topics.body:
## Description

The FA4 SM100 attention backward forms `D = rowsum(dO * O)` from the BF16 forward output. On peaked softmax rows the BF16 rounding of O makes D cancel badly, and the frozen-checkpoint study in https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/12 found genuine FP32 saved O cuts pooled hero dQ/dK error about 3x. Related: #10677.

Change (opt-in `attention_fp32_saved_output`, `--attention-fp32-saved-output all|global`): the forward writes its FP32 accumulator, returns the BF16 cast, and the custom VJP keeps the FP32 O for D. The output staging buffer aliases the query buffer, so the forward keeps two query stages and is bit-identical to production.

Kernel checks (1 GB200): forward BF16 O and LSE bitwise equal at 16k x 48 heads; two-key dQ/dK error vs FP64 100%/70.7% -> 0.30%/0.23%; 16k fwd+bwd +3.7% global, +2.3% local.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Check training numerics, step time and peak memory on the real hero config.

Setup: restore permanent step-354000, 1 GB200 rack, batch 256, optimizer sized at 2816, both LRs x sqrt(1/11), clip 1.0, steps 354000->354050, same data order.

### Links

* W&B: [ha-base](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ha-base), [ha-fp32o](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ha-fp32o)
* Branch: [larry/hero-attn-fp32o-test](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/larry/hero-attn-fp32o-test) (3434fb9b12 diagnostic flags, 8082f57415 kernel port)

## Results

See the comment below.

comments.body:
🤖 Results: ha-base vs ha-fp32o, steps 354000-354049 (50 paired steps). Page: https://claude.ai/artifact/UtNt4dNRMbhYgeTpqR2Vsa

- Paired loss delta (fp32o - base): mean +1.2e-5, SE 0.5e-5, per-step SD 3.3e-5, max |delta| 8.2e-5, cumulative +5.8e-4. Noise floor from an identical-config rerun (hero-clip-rt1 - ha-base, 33 steps): mean +1.2e-5, SD 4.0e-5. FP32 O is indistinguishable from run-to-run noise.
- Pre-clip grad norm: median 0.375 / 0.377, max 1.037 / 1.202, one clip each (base 354029, fp32o 354005). The rerun clipped at 354012 and 354029 (max 1.975), and its per-step log-ratio vs ha-base has SD 0.24 (fp32o: 0.26), so per-step norm differences are noise.
- Step time (median, steps 354005+): 13.16 s / 13.21 s (+0.4%). MFU 32.00% / 31.87%. Peak memory 123.21 / 124.71 GiB (+1.50 GiB). No NaN either arm.
- A global-layers-only arm was dropped at step 354013. Its peak was 125.70 GiB, higher than all-layers.

Verdict: the cost is about +0.4% step time and +1.5 GiB peak, with a bit-identical forward and stable training. The benefit is the gradient accuracy measured offline: two-key dQ/dK error 100%/70.7% -> 0.30%/0.23%, and per the logbook, pooled hero dQ/dK error 0.93/0.82% -> 0.28/0.25% at 330k, with global layer 15 going from 4.5% to 0.35%. Worth adopting if the hero's memory headroom absorbs 1.5 GiB. Caveat: 50 steps at 1/11 batch cannot measure a ~0.001 long-run quality effect; this test only checks numerics, cost and memory and rules out a large effect.
not viewing as priority given no measurable loss impact.

topics.title: [iris] Clarify child routing and endpoint readiness failures
topics.head: 7d9732e852dd17bb2861c965d785985323910936
topics.body:
Reject SkyRL launches from an Iris task when they retain the root launch's target cluster or parent cluster config. The error directs callers to clear those fields and submit through their coordinator's in-cluster client, instead of attempting nested federation through the hub. A different execution cluster requires a new root submission outside the task.

Report an empty endpoint registry as ConnectError(NOT_FOUND), matching the RPC path. Marin's readiness and evaluation recovery loops retry that code while propagating permission and other failures. Launch failures keep their RPC code and details, and include the operation, code and reason in the traceback; formatted RPC errors also include the code.

The directly affected CPU suites passed 180 tests, and the isolated SkyRL routing checks passed two. Broader checks encountered three host-dependent failures that also reproduce on unchanged main (GPU detection and login-shell PATH ordering), and the full affected run reached its 600-second session limit. Lint, type checks and advisory review passed.

Related to #10731, which changes launcher limits but not child routing. Part of #10768
